patient.name: Zain Rahman
patient.complaint: Itchy, dry, red rash in the elbow and knee creases, worse for 2 weeks
background: Dad has hay fever; mum had eczema as a child
Lives in Tower Hamlets; nursery 4 days a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an itchy, dry, flexural rash in an atopic patient (asthma, hay fever), or a sudden febrile blistering eruption on eczema: eczema herpeticum.

points: Zain, 4, scratches his **elbow and knee creases** all night.
Rash started on his **face and cheeks at 8 months**.
He has **asthma**; dad has hay fever.
Worse since the cold weather and a new washing powder.

steps.lead: A chronic itchy rash that began **before age 2** in a child: this is **atopic eczema**.
Zain's **asthma**, dad's hay fever and mum's eczema give him a strong atopic background. Many such families carry a **filaggrin** mutation.

points: Dry skin all over; red, **poorly demarcated** patches.
Both antecubital and popliteal fossae: thickened, leathery skin.
Face now clear; no silvery scale; nails normal.

steps.lead: Zain's rash has moved from the **face** (infant pattern) to the **flexures** (child pattern), with lichenification from scratching.

steps.q: Zain's rash sits in his elbow creases. Which age pattern is this?
o: Contact pattern: only where the trigger touched
steps.r: Infants get **face, scalp and extensor** eczema; older children and adults get **flexural** eczema (antecubital, popliteal, neck).

steps.title: The atopic march
steps.caption: Eczema is often the first step. Asking about asthma and hay fever is part of the diagnosis.

steps.lead: Watch Zain for **eczema herpeticum**: fever plus sudden monomorphic blisters on eczema is an emergency. Infected eczema is commoner.

steps.text: **Eczema herpeticum** blisters are all the same size and age (**monomorphic**) and punched out. Chickenpox lesions appear in crops at different stages.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical diagnosis), patch testing for suspected contact allergy, or same-day referral for eczema herpeticum.

steps.q: Zain's mum asks for a blood test to 'prove' it is eczema. What confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: Atopic eczema is a **clinical diagnosis** from history and examination. Tests are only for specific questions.

steps.lead: Zain needs **no tests**: an itchy, flexural, relapsing rash starting before 2 in an atopic child is enough.

steps.title: Bloods taken at a previous allergy clinic
steps.text: IgE is often raised in atopic eczema but it is **not needed** to make the diagnosis.

visual.title: Zain's total IgE
visual.label: Zain 820
visual.caption: Raised IgE reflects the Th2-driven atopic response. It supports, but does not make, the diagnosis.

steps.lead: If Zain's rash flared only where something touched him, a **patch test** would look for allergic contact dermatitis. Eczema herpeticum means **same-day** referral.

steps.text: Patch testing is for **allergic contact dermatitis** (type IV). Skin prick and IgE tests are for immediate food or aeroallergen allergy. Neither diagnoses atopic eczema.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': emollients plus the right-potency topical steroid, tacrolimus when steroids fail, and IV aciclovir with same-day referral for eczema herpeticum.

steps.lead: The base of Zain's plan is **emollients every day**, even when clear, applied after his bath.
For this flare, Zain gets emollients plus a **mild** steroid, **hydrocortisone 1%**, the NICE choice for the face and flexures.

visual.title: Topical steroid potency ladder
visual.label: Zain: hydrocortisone 1%
visual.caption: Match potency to severity and site. Face and flexures: the lowest that works.

steps.lead: If Zain's flare had widespread **excoriations**, a short course of **clobetasone butyrate 0.05%** and **wet wraps** would follow.
If Zain's eczema stayed severe despite steroids, a **topical calcineurin inhibitor** such as **tacrolimus** would be next, then systemic therapy.

points: Three weeks later, Zain's mum kissed him while she had a **cold sore**.
Overnight: clusters of **painful, punched-out blisters** on his neck and chest.
He is **febrile**, miserable and off his food.

steps.q: Zain has eczema herpeticum. Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral flucloxacillin and review in 48 hours
Potent topical steroid to the blisters
Same-day hospital referral and IV aciclovir
steps.r: Eczema herpeticum is a **dermatological emergency**: same-day referral and **IV aciclovir**. Steroids on the area make HSV spread.

steps.lead: Zain starts **IV aciclovir**. If his eczema were weeping with golden crusts (Staph aureus), he would need **flucloxacillin**.
Zain's care follows **NICE CG57** (atopic eczema in under 12s) and the NICE CKS eczema pathway.

visual.title: Zain's itch score with treatment
visual.caption: Steroid settles the flare in 1 to 2 weeks; regular emollients keep it down.

steps.text: Treat with steroid until the flare settles, then **step down**. Emollients continue forever, and are used in far larger amounts than steroid.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the filaggrin mutation and barrier failure, the Th2/IgE response, why scratching causes lichenification, and why HSV spreads so widely.

steps.lead: Zain's skin loses water and lets allergens in because faulty **filaggrin** weakens the **stratum corneum**.

steps.title: From barrier failure to flare
steps.caption: The itch-scratch cycle keeps the barrier broken.

steps.lead: Allergens getting through Zain's barrier trigger a **Th2** response, which is why his **IgE is 820**.
Zain's asthma and dad's hay fever are linked by the **atopic march**: shared genes and immunology.
Zain's thick, leathery elbow creases are **lichenification** from months of scratching.

steps.q: Why did his mum's cold sore spread so widely over Zain's skin?
o: HSV is more virulent in children
The broken barrier and local immune dysfunction let HSV spread
steps.r: Atopic skin has a **broken barrier** and **impaired local immunity**, so HSV disseminates across the eczema.

steps.lead: This is why Zain's herpes spread over his neck and chest within a day.
Zain has darker skin, so his mum should know steroids can cause **depigmentation** by inhibiting melanocytes.

steps.text: Lighter patches after steroid in darker skin are often **post-inflammatory hypopigmentation** or steroid depigmentation; both usually recover.

mcq.q: Which gene is classically mutated in atopic eczema?
Where is atopic eczema typically found in older children and adults?
Which describes the edge of atopic eczema compared with psoriasis?
mcq.r: Eczema is **poorly demarcated**; psoriasis is well demarcated.

mcq.q: How is atopic eczema usually diagnosed?
Which test is used for suspected allergic contact dermatitis?
mcq.r: **Patch testing** detects delayed (type IV) contact allergy.

mcq.q: What is the NICE mild-potency topical steroid for the face and flexures?
Which is a topical calcineurin inhibitor used in severe eczema?
Which T-helper response drives atopic eczema?

technique.stem: A 19 year old man has a 3 month history of an itchy rash on the backs of his knees and the front of his elbows. The skin is dry and thickened, with poorly demarcated redness and excoriations. He has asthma and hay fever. His nails are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a chronic itchy rash: site, edge and background decide.
Flexural, itchy, dry, lichenified, poorly demarcated, atopic history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Flexural itchy rash in an atopic patient: **atopic dermatitis**.

elim: Confined to where an allergen touches; flexures in both arms and legs fit atopy.
Well-demarcated, scaly, extensor plaques, often with nail changes.
Burrows in finger webs and genitals, often household contacts.
Greasy scale on the scalp, face and chest, not flexural limbs.

steps.x: **B. Atopic dermatitis.** Flexures + itch + asthma/hay fever = atopic eczema.

technique.stem: A 6 year old girl has had an itchy, dry rash in her elbow and knee creases since she was 1. It flares in winter. She has asthma. Examination shows poorly demarcated, excoriated patches in both antecubital fossae.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnostic test for a classic picture.
Onset before 2, relapsing, atopic, flexural.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Typical atopic eczema needs **no test**: it is clinical.

elim: Often raised but not needed and not diagnostic.
Only for diagnostic doubt; not for typical eczema.
For suspected allergic contact dermatitis, not typical atopic eczema.
For suspected immediate food or aeroallergen allergy.

steps.x: **A. No investigation: clinical diagnosis.** Investigate only when something is atypical.

technique.stem: A 3 year old boy with atopic eczema has a 1 day history of a painful rash of clustered, punched-out erosions and blisters over his eczema on his face and neck. He is irritable and not eating. His temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 150 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of a febrile blistering eruption on eczema.
Eczema, monomorphic punched-out lesions, fever, unwell child.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Eczema herpeticum**: same-day referral and **IV aciclovir**.

elim: Treats bacterial infection; this is HSV.
Steroid on HSV lesions spreads the infection.
For localised impetigo-like bacterial infection.
For severe eczema flares, not infection.

steps.x: **A. IV aciclovir.** Never steroids on suspected herpes.

technique.stem: A 2 year old girl has atopic eczema. Her serum IgE is markedly raised and she has started wheezing. Her mother asks why her skin lets in so many allergens.
technique.q: Which is the most likely underlying mechanism?
o: Excess keratinocyte turnover driven by Th17
Fungal overgrowth on the skin surface

steps.x: Mechanism question: why is the barrier leaky?
Atopic child, high IgE, atopic march, leaky barrier.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Filaggrin** loss weakens the stratum corneum, letting allergens in and driving Th2/IgE.

elim: That is bullous pemphigoid.
That is psoriasis.
That is candidiasis or tinea, not atopy.
That is vasculitis or lupus.

steps.x: **E. Loss-of-function mutation in filaggrin.** Barrier failure first, Th2 inflammation second.

practice.stem:
A 9 year old boy has a 4 month history of an intensely itchy rash in both elbow creases and behind his knees. It keeps him awake. He has asthma and his father has hay fever. The skin is dry, thickened and excoriated with poorly demarcated redness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 98/62 mmHg.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An intensely itchy, poorly demarcated, lichenified flexural rash with asthma and family atopy is atopic dermatitis. Psoriasis is well demarcated on extensors.

steps.x: Diagnosis: site, itch and background.

clues: elbow creases and behind his knees
steps.x: Flexural, very itchy, atopic family, lichenified, raised IgE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Atopic dermatitis.**

elim: Would follow contact with a specific allergen; not symmetrical flexures.
Well-demarcated scaly extensor plaques, little itch.
Burrows in finger webs, family contacts, itch worse at night.
Greasy scale on the scalp and face.

steps.x: **B. Atopic dermatitis.** Flexures plus atopy.

practice.stem: A 7 month old girl has a 6 week history of an itchy rash on her cheeks, scalp and the fronts of her knees. She rubs her face against the cot. The skin is dry and red with some weeping. Her mother has asthma. Her temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 128 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Infants get atopic eczema on the face, scalp and extensors, and it is itchy. Seborrhoeic dermatitis gives greasy, non-itchy cradle cap.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an infant.

clues: cheeks, scalp and the fronts of her knees
steps.x: Itchy face, scalp and extensor rash in an infant with family atopy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infant-pattern **atopic dermatitis**.

elim: Golden crusted lesions, often around the mouth, not chronic and dry.
Rare; well demarcated, usually in the napkin area.
Greasy yellow scale (cradle cap), not itchy, child undisturbed.
Burrows and papules, palms and soles in infants.

steps.x: **A. Atopic dermatitis.** Infants: face, scalp and extensors; older: flexures.

practice.stem: A 2 year old boy with atopic eczema has a 1 day history of a rapidly spreading painful rash over his eczema on his chest and neck. There are many uniform, punched-out erosions and small blisters. His aunt has a cold sore. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 150 bpm and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Uniform punched-out erosions on eczematous skin with fever after HSV contact is eczema herpeticum. Chickenpox lesions are at different stages.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a febrile blistering rash on eczema.
Eczema, monomorphic punched-out lesions, HSV contact, fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Eczema herpeticum** (HSV-1).

elim: Gives weeping and golden crusts, not monomorphic punched-out vesicles.
Lesions in crops at different stages, not confined to eczema.
Honey-crusted lesions, child usually well.
Drug-induced, with mucosal involvement and target lesions.

steps.x: **C. Eczema herpeticum.** Monomorphic punched-out lesions on eczema with fever.

practice.stem: A 5 year old girl with atopic eczema has a 1 day history of widespread blisters and erosions over her eczema with fever and malaise. Her temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 140 bpm. A swab is sent for viral PCR.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Eczema herpeticum is caused by HSV-1. Coxsackievirus gives eczema coxsackium, which does not respond to IV aciclovir.

steps.x: Organism question.
Febrile, widespread blisters on eczema; viral swab.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Eczema herpeticum: **HSV-1**.

elim: Causes eczema coxsackium, a less common mimic that does not respond to aciclovir.
Causes infected eczema with crusting, not monomorphic blisters.
Causes impetigo or cellulitis.
Chickenpox; lesions in crops anywhere.

steps.x: **B. Herpes simplex virus type 1.** Coxsackievirus is the mimic that aciclovir will not help.

practice.stem:
An 8 year old boy with atopic eczema has a 4 day history of his eczema becoming weeping and painful, with golden-yellow crusts on both forearms. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 37.4°C.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Weeping eczema with golden crusts in a well child is secondary bacterial infection, typically Staphylococcus aureus, treated with flucloxacillin.

steps.x: Organism question for infected eczema.
Weeping, golden crusts, well child, mildly raised CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Secondary bacterial infection: **Staph aureus**.

elim: Gives moist red rash with satellite lesions in skin folds.
Gives punched-out blisters and fever.
Uncommon in eczema; green discharge.
Tinea: annular scaly rash.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** Treat with flucloxacillin.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has had eczema since infancy. She has asthma. She scratches her elbow creases daily. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her elbow creases?
practice.e: Repeated scratching thickens the epidermis, giving leathery lichenified skin with excoriations. Silvery scale and nail pitting are psoriasis.

steps.x: Most likely finding question.
Chronic eczema with daily scratching of a flexure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic scratching thickens skin: **lichenification**.

elim: Scabies.
Psoriasis.
Erythema multiforme.
Psoriasis on extensors.

steps.x: **B. Lichenification with excoriations.**

practice.stem:
A 5 year old boy has had an itchy rash in his elbow and knee creases since he was 9 months old. He has asthma. The rash is dry and poorly demarcated. His mother asks which test will confirm the diagnosis.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Atopic eczema is a clinical diagnosis. A raised IgE is common but not required or diagnostic.

steps.x: Diagnostic test for a typical case.
Onset before 2, flexural, atopic: textbook.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clinical diagnosis**; no test needed.

elim: Supportive at best, as here; not diagnostic.
Not needed for typical eczema.
For suspected contact allergy.
For fungal infection.

steps.x: **A. No investigation: clinical diagnosis.** A raised IgE does not make the diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 28 year old hairdresser has atopic eczema since childhood. Over 3 months, eczema has developed on the backs of both hands and worsens at work despite gloves. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: A work-related hand eczema suggests allergic contact dermatitis (e.g. hair dye), so skin patch testing is indicated. Prick tests detect immediate IgE allergy.

steps.x: Investigation of a suspected trigger.
Occupational exposure; hands; work-related.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Suspected **allergic contact dermatitis**: patch test.

elim: Raised in atopy and does not identify a contact allergen.
Not needed to find a trigger.
For immediate (IgE) allergy, not delayed contact allergy.
For tinea; the work link points to an allergen.

steps.x: **C. Skin patch testing.** Patch test for contact allergy (type IV).

practice.stem: A 3 year old girl with atopic eczema has a flare with red, dry, itchy patches on her cheeks and in her elbow creases. She uses an emollient twice daily. There is no weeping or crusting. Her temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 112 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Continue emollient and add hydrocortisone 1% cream
practice.e: NICE advises emollients plus a mild topical steroid (hydrocortisone 1%) for the face and flexures. Very potent steroids are never used on a child's face.

steps.x: Initial management of a flare.
Uninfected flare on face and flexures in a child.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emollient plus **mild** topical steroid: **hydrocortisone 1%**.

elim: Very potent: never for a child's face.
No sign of infection.
Systemic steroid is not used for a simple flare.
Second line when steroids fail or are unsuitable.

steps.x: **B. Continue emollient and add hydrocortisone 1% cream.** Lowest potency that works on face and flexures.

practice.stem:
A 4 year old boy with atopic eczema has a 1 day history of painful clusters of punched-out erosions on his neck. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 146 bpm and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. He is irritable.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Eczema herpeticum needs same-day hospital assessment and IV aciclovir. Topical steroids spread the virus; antibacterials miss HSV.

steps.x: Initial management of a febrile blistering eruption on eczema.
Eczema, punched-out erosions, fever, tachycardia, raised CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Eczema herpeticum: same-day referral, **IV aciclovir**.

elim: For bacterial infection; this is HSV.
For fungal infection.
Worsens HSV.
For localised bacterial infection.

steps.x: **A. IV aciclovir.**

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has severe atopic eczema on her eyelids and face. It has not settled with emollients and hydrocortisone 1%, and she is worried about steroid skin thinning. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus) are used for severe eczema, especially on the face, when steroids fail or atrophy is a concern.

steps.x: Next step when mild steroid fails on the face.
Severe, facial, steroid-sparing wanted.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Topical calcineurin inhibitor: **tacrolimus**.

elim: Very potent: causes atrophy on the face.
Systemic therapy comes after topical options fail.
Not for routine eczema control; rebound flare.
Used for severe childhood eczema on the limbs and trunk, not eyelids.

steps.x: **D. Topical tacrolimus.** Steroid-sparing; no skin atrophy.

practice.stem: A 6 month old boy has dry, itchy eczema on his face. His father and sister have eczema and asthma. Genetic testing in the family shows a loss-of-function mutation in a skin barrier protein. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 130 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his dry, leaky skin?
o: Impaired stratum corneum formation from filaggrin loss
practice.e: Filaggrin loss-of-function impairs stratum corneum formation, increasing transepidermal water loss and allergen penetration.

steps.x: Mechanism question about the barrier.

clues: loss-of-function mutation in a skin barrier protein
steps.x: Atopic family; barrier protein mutation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Filaggrin** loss impairs the stratum corneum: water out, allergens in.

elim: That is pemphigus.
That is dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
Linked to acne and seborrhoeic dermatitis.
That is psoriasis.

steps.x: **D. Impaired stratum corneum formation from filaggrin loss.**

glossary.Atopic dermatitis: Chronic itchy inflammatory skin disease linked to atopy; same as atopic eczema.
glossary.Atopy: An inherited tendency to make IgE to harmless allergens, causing eczema, asthma and hay fever.
glossary.Atopic march: The typical progression from infant eczema to food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis.
glossary.Atopic triad: Eczema, asthma and allergic rhinitis occurring together.
glossary.Filaggrin: A skin protein that helps build the stratum corneum barrier; mutated in many with eczema.
glossary.Stratum corneum: The outermost dead-cell layer of the epidermis that forms the skin barrier.
glossary.Transepidermal water loss: Water evaporating through the skin; increased when the barrier is faulty.
glossary.Lichenification: Thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated markings from chronic scratching.
glossary.Excoriation: A scratch mark where the skin surface has been scraped off.
glossary.Flexural: In the skin creases on the bending side of joints, such as inner elbows and backs of knees.
glossary.Antecubital fossa: The hollow at the front of the elbow.
glossary.Popliteal fossa: The hollow at the back of the knee.
glossary.Extensor surfaces: The outer side of joints, such as the backs of elbows and fronts of knees.
glossary.Poorly demarcated: With a blurred edge that merges into normal skin.
glossary.Eczema herpeticum: Widespread HSV-1 infection of eczematous skin with fever; a dermatological emergency.
glossary.Eczema coxsackium: Coxsackievirus infection of eczematous skin; mimics eczema herpeticum but does not respond to aciclovir.
glossary.Monomorphic: All lesions look the same and are at the same stage.
glossary.HSV-1: Herpes simplex virus type 1, the cause of cold sores and eczema herpeticum.
glossary.IgE: The antibody class behind allergy; often raised in atopic eczema.
glossary.Th2: T-helper type 2 cells, which drive allergic inflammation and IgE production.
glossary.Emollient: A moisturiser that softens skin and restores the barrier.
glossary.Hydrocortisone 1%: A mild-potency topical corticosteroid, safe for the face and flexures.
glossary.Clobetasone butyrate: A moderate-potency topical corticosteroid (0.05%); not to be confused with clobetasol.
glossary.Clobetasol propionate: A very potent topical corticosteroid; avoid on the face and in children.
glossary.Wet wrapping: Damp bandages over emollient or steroid to boost absorption in severe childhood eczema.
glossary.Tacrolimus: A topical calcineurin inhibitor used as a steroid-sparing treatment in severe eczema.
glossary.Pimecrolimus: A topical calcineurin inhibitor, like tacrolimus, used in eczema.
glossary.Calcineurin inhibitor: Drug that blocks T-cell activation; used topically in eczema to avoid steroid side effects.
glossary.Aciclovir: Antiviral drug for herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections.
glossary.Depigmentation: Loss of skin colour, here from steroid inhibition of melanocytes.
glossary.Patch test: Allergens taped on the back for 48 hours to detect delayed contact allergy.
glossary.Allergic contact dermatitis: Type IV hypersensitivity eczema where an allergen touches the skin.
glossary.Keratinocyte: The main cell type of the epidermis.
